question.text: The radius of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>nd</mi></msup></math> orbit of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>He</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></math> of Bohr's model is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and that of fourth orbit of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>Be</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></math> is represented as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>.</mo></math> Now the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>:</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math> The value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math> is _____.

solution.text:
The formula to calculate the radius r of any nth Bohr's orbit is given by

r=r0n2Z   ...1

where, r0 is Bohr's radius, n is the principal quantum number and Z is the atomic number.

Thus, for Helium ion,

r1=r0222= 2r0   ...2

And, for the Beryllium ion,

r2=r0424=4r0   ...3

Divide equation (3) by equation (2) to obtain the required ratio.

r2r1=4r02r0=2

Hence, x=2.
